skill.name: Can I trust this source?
skill.why: Some texts are written to trick you. Clues show you who to trust.
skill.how: Check who wrote it, what they gain, their evidence, and how recent it is.

steps.say: I'm reading about snakes at camp. First check: who wrote it?

show.text: Written by Dr Lee, a snake scientist.
Written by Vinnie, who sells snake spray.
show.nudge: Selling spray doesn't make Vinnie a snake expert. Who studies snakes?
Who is NoName123? You can't tell what they know.

steps.ask: Tap the writer who really knows about snakes.
steps.win: Yes! Dr Lee studies snakes. Ask: who wrote it, and do they know the topic?

steps.say: Next check: what do they gain? Here's Vinnie's page.
steps.ask: What does Vinnie gain if you believe him?

options.text: He wins a prize for writing.
options.reason: There's no prize. Look at what's for sale.

options.text: He sells more spray.
Nothing. He just likes snakes.
options.reason: Read the end. What is Vinnie selling?

steps.win: Yes! Scared readers buy spray. When a writer gains, that's a warning sign.

steps.say: Next check: do they show evidence, or just say it?

show.nudge: 'Trust me' is just saying it. Where's the proof?

show.text: In our test, 40 of 50 snakes stayed away.

show.nudge: Who is everyone? Nobody counted anything.

steps.win: Yes! A test with numbers is evidence you can check. 'Trust me' is not.

steps.say: Careful! Old pages can still be right. Age matters for things that change, like beaches.
steps.ask: Which page from nine years ago should worry you most?

options.text: one saying the moon goes round Earth
options.reason: The moon still goes round Earth. Some facts don't change.

options.text: one saying the beach has no jellyfish
one saying bilbies have long ears
options.reason: Bilbies' ears haven't changed in nine years. Old is fine here.

steps.win: Yes! Jellyfish come and go, so old beach news could be wrong now. Ask: could it have changed?

steps.say: Careful! Vinnie gains from sales, but he might still be right. How can you find out?
steps.ask: How could Zed check Vinnie's claim?

options.text: Read Vinnie's page again, slowly.
options.reason: Reading it twice won't change it. Who else could Zed check with?

options.text: Ask Vinnie if he's sure.
options.reason: Vinnie gains from your fear. Ask someone with nothing to sell.

options.text: Read the ranger's snake count.

steps.win: Yes! Best check of all: what do other sources say? If the ranger agrees, Vinnie was right.

steps.say: Now use every check. Which source should I trust most?
steps.ask: Which should Zed trust most about snakes at camp this week?

options.text: the camp ranger's snake count from Monday
Vinnie's ad: 'Snakes everywhere!'
options.reason: Vinnie gains from sales, and he shows no count.

options.text: a snake book from 1990
options.reason: A scientist may have written it, but snake numbers change. Is it about this week?

steps.win: Yes! The ranger knows snakes, gains nothing, counted them, and it's new.

terms.means: The writer knows the topic, gains nothing, shows evidence, and it's up to date.
A clue to check somewhere else: a seller, no proof, old news, or no name.

encounters.frame: Gus wants a RoboPup, a robot dog. The Proofanna found two reports that disagree about its battery.
encounters.text: REPORT A, from PupTech, the company that designed and builds RoboPup. Posted last week. 'RoboPup is the most advanced robot pet ever made. Its long-life battery lasts for days, so the fun never has to stop! RoboPup can sit, roll over and fetch, and it never needs feeding or walking. Our engineers have spent five years making it perfect. Ninety-nine per cent of kids love RoboPup, and thousands of happy comments online agree. Order yours today and get a free squeaky bone.' REPORT B, from Fair Go Testers, a group that is paid by its members and accepts no money from toy companies. Posted last month. 'We bought fifty RoboPups from ordinary shops and tested them for three months. On average, the battery lasted nine hours from a full charge, not days. After eight weeks, eleven of the fifty batteries would no longer charge at all. We also asked thirty families to use RoboPup at home and keep a diary. Most children loved it for the first week, but several said it became boring once the battery kept running flat. RoboPup is fun to play with, and it learnt tricks quickly, but buyers should know that the battery is its weak point. Our full results, robot by robot, are printed on the back page.'
encounters.prompt: Which statement best explains why Report B is more trustworthy?
encounters.success: Fair Go Testers gain nothing from sales, and they show detailed results from fifty robots.

options.text: Its testers gain nothing from sales, and they show results from fifty robots.
It was posted more recently than Report A, so its results are more up to date.
options.reason: Report B was posted last month and Report A last week, so B is older.

options.text: It quotes thousands of happy comments online, so lots of people agree with it.
options.reason: Report A mentions the happy comments, not Report B. Comments aren't careful evidence anyway.

options.text: Its writers designed and built RoboPup, so they understand the battery best.
options.reason: That describes Report A. A company gains when its own product looks good.

parts: THE LADY OF THE LIGHT. On stormy nights, they say, a woman in a long grey coat can be seen at the top of the old Bluster Rock lighthouse, holding a lantern out over the black water. Her name was Edith Crane, and she was the keeper's daughter. One winter, her father's boat failed to come home, and Edith kept the lamp burning for forty nights, waiting for him. He never returned. Ever since, sailors have reported a flickering light in the tower, long after the lamp was switched off for good. Some say that if you stand at the bottom of the stairs at midnight, you can hear her calling her father's name. Others claim the lantern swings even when there is no wind at all. The old keeper's cottage still stands beside the tower, its windows boarded up.

parts.tap: The writer says that every local knows the story is true.
parts.reason: That is a good reason. 'Everyone knows' is a claim with no proof.

parts.tap: No photos, diaries or records of the ghost are given.
parts.reason: That is a good reason. A ghost claim with no evidence is hard to trust.

parts.tap: The article was first published more than sixty years ago.
The article was written by Captain Morrow's Ghost Tours, which runs nightly trips to the lighthouse at forty dollars a ticket.
parts.reason: That is a good reason. The tour company sells more tickets if you believe.

encounters.frame: Zed has ten dollars of pocket money for a Creature charity. He compared two donation pages.
encounters.text: PAGE A: Bluster Rock Wombat Rescue. 'Every dollar helps sick wombats.' Our money is checked every year by an outside accountant, a money checker with no link to the rescue. Our latest report, from last year, lists what the money paid for: 412 bags of joey formula, a new trailer and two heat lamps. The ranger's office also lists us as a rescue it works with. The page has one grey photo of a wombat in a basket and no videos. PAGE B: The Creature Care Fund, run by Dazza, a streamer with a gold microphone. Posted this morning. 'Every dollar goes straight to Creatures!' The page has twelve bright videos of happy Creatures, music, and a giant gold donate button. Dazza says his own team counts the money. No outside checker is named, and there are no receipts or reports. The comments are full of hearts, and one says, 'Dazza is a legend!' Nobody in the comments says what the money bought. Zed wants every cent of his ten dollars to reach an animal, not a gold microphone.

encounters.success: An outsider with nothing to gain checks Page A's money, and it shows what the money bought.

encounters.frame: Tully read a rave review of the Dusty Possums' new album. Zed wrote a trust check, but got one part wrong.
encounters.text: ALBUM REVIEW: 'RED DIRT ROAD' by The Dusty Possums. Posted this week. Let me be clear: this is the greatest album ever recorded on Bluster Rock, and possibly anywhere. From the first twang of the banjo to the final crash of the drums, every one of its twelve songs is a number-one hit waiting to happen. The band formed four years ago in a shearing shed outside town, and this is their second album. The drumming on 'Galah Galah' is so fast that I worried the drummer might take off. Song seven, a slow ballad about a lost cattle dog, made me cry twice. There is not one weak moment from start to finish. Critics who say the middle songs sound the same simply haven't listened properly. Lead singer Mabel Dunn's voice is like honey poured over gravel, and the title track will have you dancing in your kitchen. If you buy one album this year, make it this one, and buy a second copy for a friend. I can't recommend it highly enough. You can order it from the band's own shop, where signed copies are thirty dollars. Review by Jett Ramone, manager of The Dusty Possums, who is paid a share of every album sold.

encounters.frame: After the big flood, Mo wants to know if the tap water on Bluster Rock is safe to drink. The Proofanna gathered three sources.
encounters.prompt: Put the sources in order, from most to least trustworthy about today's tap water.
encounters.success: Today's tests first. The leaflet's advice fits any flood. The old article was about the last flood, not this one.

items: The town water authority's test results, posted this morning, from samples taken at twelve taps across Bluster Rock.
A health department leaflet, printed eight years ago, which says that after any flood, tap water should be boiled until new tests say it is safe.
A Bugle article, printed eight years ago, which says the water was safe to drink again a week after the last flood.
body.reason: Old is fine for advice that never changes. Old news about the water back then says nothing about now.

encounters.frame: Players keep twisting their ankles on the new Bluster Rock oval. Tully found two articles that disagree about why.
encounters.text: ARTICLE A, from Grassmaster Turf, the company that laid the oval's new artificial grass. Posted last year. 'Grassmaster Turf is the safest playing surface money can buy. No injuries have ever been linked to our turf, and players everywhere love the bounce. Our turf is made from the finest materials and has been laid at more than two hundred grounds. It stays green all year, even in the hottest summer, and never needs mowing. Clubs that switch to Grassmaster never look back.' ARTICLE B, by Dr Kim Lau, physiotherapist for the Bluster Rock footy club. Posted last week. 'This season, I treated twenty-three ankle injuries from games on the new turf. Last season, on the old grass, I treated six. Most of the injuries happened late in games, and most were on the wing near the clubrooms, where the surface feels hardest underfoot. Several players have also told me their boots grip too tightly when they turn. That is a worrying jump, although it does not yet prove that the turf is the cause, because we also have more players this year. Together with the council, I am now measuring how hard the surface is in different spots, and I will share the results with every club member. Until then, players should wear boots with shorter studs.'
encounters.prompt: Which is the best reason to be careful of Article A?
encounters.success: Grassmaster laid the turf, so it would lose business if the turf were blamed. Check what others say.

options.text: Article A says the turf stays green the whole year, which sounds too good to be true.
options.reason: Artificial grass really does stay green. Look at who wrote Article A, and what they would lose.
